newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Inside Canberra-Fischer on wheat and sugar.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Inside Canberra-Fischer on wheat and sugar.

text.p: Card shops and newsagents are small beer compared with big industries like wheat and sugar.
Hilmer competition policy was a creation of the Keating government.
In opposition the National Party (particularly in Queensland) was positively hostile to it.

This is what led the coalition in opposition to promise retention of the single desk (monopoly) export power of the Australian Wheat Board through exemption from the TP Act and also for Fischer to promise the sugar industry exemption.

In the House (September 18) Fischer was asked by De-Anne Kelly (National, Qld) whether the government would honor its commitment "not to overarch or override" the current Queensland government review of the sugar industry if it found the regulatory arrangements - acquisition and single desk selling for the domestic and export market - should be maintained.
Fischer said that part of the government's "sustainable approach" to agricultural exports included the "cast-iron retention" of the single desk selling for wheat.
Dealing with the question he said - "I reiterate what the prime minister has said; that is, the federal government will not interfere or overarch state legislation in this regard."
But this piece of Fischerspeak suggesting the states can do as they wish is dodging the point.

The fact is that the states, including Queensland, have signed up to a deal on competition policy with the commonwealth whereby they will be delivered billions of dollars by the feds if they come through on competition policy.
When Queensland signed (admittedly under the previous Labor government) there was no caveat that sugar and wheat were excluded from the deal.

As Treasury officials made clear at last week's Senate Economics Legislation Committee, the money will be delivered to the states if the National Competition Council reports that a state has complied with the agreement.
Brian Cassidy, First Assistant Secretary, Structural Policy Division of Treasury explained to the committee that the commonwealth treasurer could accept or reject the recommendation of the Council.

But Inside Canberra makes the point that if Queensland was found by the Council not to have carried out its obligations because of, say, refusing to give up single desk selling of sugar, it would be politically difficult for the treasurer to override the Council and give Queensland money it would not be entitled to.
The other states which had complied would not meekly sit back and let Queensland get an undeserved handout.
In short there is a long way to go before the coalition delivers on its "cast iron" promise of retaining single desk selling for wheat and Fischer's similar promise to the sugar industry.
(Views are those of Inside Canberra, not Reuters)
